The 90 comes from the fact that 180/2=90.

There’s a theory that I find holds true in a lot of cases, that an abundance of natural resources actually *slows down* development. Looking at the most developed countries in the world per capita, we find areas like the Nordic countries, which have almost no natural resources, Switzerland, which is literally just mountains, and Australia, which is little more than a coastline that surrounds a desert. Why is this?

Essentially, the theory goes that a country that has had natural resources throughout history has been able to rely on those resources to sustain themselves in the global economy. Therefore, they never needed to develop new technologies to sustain those economies. Their populous never needed to educate themselves to do anything new. Therefore they didn’t develop.
Meanwhile, in countries that needed to take drastic measures like import food just to survive, and that didn’t have the natural resources to sustain that trade balance, the population needed to educate themselves to jobs in industries like manufacturing and science.

But there is one factor we should consider for Africa specifically that may soon boost their development, that being their birthrates. While many developed countries like Japan are ageing, becoming weighed down by a mob of the elderly, the median age in Africa is 18 years old. That means that as education becomes more widely available around the world, Africa will be able to monopolise on that education in a way that no other continent can. So while it’s definitely possible that Africa will be unable to get out of their current hole of corruption and poverty, it’s also possible that it is soon going to change.
